title: Judge B: product and design judge
brief:
You are a judge for the PayPal AI Hackathon on Devpost (2026). Your background: product designer and startup founder who has judged many hackathons; you care about whether real people would use it, whether the experience is clear, and whether the pitch lands. Judge the project "Join" strictly and fairly. Do not edit any files.

Official judging (Rules §6):
- Stage One (pass/fail): "reasonably fits the theme and reasonably applies the required APIs/SDKs" (an app that integrates the PayPal developer platform, sandbox, along with an AI tool, model, or platform).
- Stage Two: five criteria of EQUAL weight, each scored 1-10: Technological Implementation, Design, Potential Impact, Innovation (quality of the idea), Presentation. Ties break on Technological Implementation first.
- Judges may judge from the text description, images and video alone. The demo video is NOT recorded yet: score Presentation as the submission currently stands (text, docs, screenshots), and say what the video must do.

Materials:
- The repository at D:\paypal\join: README.md, docs/SUBMISSION.md (the Devpost text), docs/JUDGING.md (the team's claims: check them), docs/demo-video-script.md, docs/screenshots/*.png (look at them: are they current and convincing?), and the web app source in web/src (pages and components) to understand the UX.
- The app runs on the local network at http://192.168.31.145:8799. Use the built-in browser tools (mcp__Claude_Browser__*; load with ToolSearch if deferred) in your OWN new tab to look around as a first-time user: http://192.168.31.145:8799/demo?as=priya&go=activity , the "No agent? Ask Join's" drawer, Plans, Map, Limits, Connect, Venue view, a receipt page. You may chat with the drawer and look at options, but do NOT click "Go ahead"/"Negotiate"/"Book"/accept/pay/review or any button that commits money or posts content, and never enter credentials or personal data. Keep it under ~40 browser actions.

Report (concise, plain text):
1. Stage One: pass/fail and why.
2. For each of the five criteria: score 1-10, the strongest evidence, and the biggest weaknesses a skeptical judge would raise (UX confusion, unclear value, jargon, too many features, outdated screenshots, etc.).
3. Total out of 50 and a one-line verdict against strong competition.
4. The three changes that would raise your scores the most before the Nov 12 deadline, each with the criterion it moves and roughly how much. Include specific advice for the 3-minute video.
Be specific and critical; inflated praise is useless.

14	## 1. Technological Implementation
15	
16	**Nine PayPal products in one money flow, each doing a job only it can do.**
17	
18	| PayPal | What it does in Join | Code |
19	|---|---|---|
20	| Orders v2, intent `AUTHORIZE`, one order per payer | The organizer guarantees the whole price; each friend authorizes their own share | `api/src/pay/settle.js` `startPayment` |
21	| Authorizations: partial `final_capture`, void | At the lock, each share is captured, and the organizer's authorization only for what's left (whoever didn't pay); a decline or a release voids | `settle.js` `lock`, `release` |
22	| Captures: refund | Cancelling more than 24 hours ahead refunds everyone | `settle.js` `refundAll` |
23	| Payouts | The venue is paid after the game, net of fees; an organizer is paid back; a venue's extras are paid out | `settle.js` `tick` |

finalMessage:
**Stage One: pass.** Join integrates Orders v2, Authorizations, Captures, Payouts, Vault, Invoicing and JS SDK v6 on the PayPal sandbox. It also has the Agent Toolkit back office and MCP and A2A agent interfaces, with Claude as the user's agent and Qwen for the website agent. It fits "AI agents + PayPal" fully. I did not test the sandbox itself. In my sessions the activity log said "PayPal sandbox ... test card (a demo stand-in for their approval)", so the payments I saw were test-card stand-ins.

**What I found in the live app** (Priya demo, about 25 actions)
- **Venue view crashed the whole app.** I clicked Venue view, then a venue, and the page went blank. The console showed "Uncaught Error: Invalid start/end dates. Start date must be less than end date" from PlaceScheduler (the Bryntum Scheduler). My browser is on a UTC+8 clock while the town is Los Angeles. The README says times are the town's "wherever the viewer is," which this contradicts. The Bryntum scheduler is the sponsor-prize piece, and a judge in a non-US timezone could hit this.
- **The first-time drawer experience is a dead end.** I asked for badminton with 3 friends. All three options read "your weekly limit leaves $0.00 that week · too far over your limit to haggle." The demo state has been used up, so a fresh judge cannot see the hero flow.
- **Activity is full of test debris.** It shows "offered $0.01", "tried to accept $31.80: This negotiation is agreed." and "offered $20.00: This negotiation is agreed." It also shows three bookings "locked (the time to pay ran out)" where friends show "not started."
- **Plans is confusing.** A booking reads "Paid And Locked" (odd capitalization) while three of four players are "not started." The organizer silently paid for everyone. A review form already appears on a booking that is a day away.
- **Smaller issues.** The Map first loads empty with a stray ". Venues are pins" sentence. The receipt's transparency-log row flashed a red X before showing a pass; the final text read fine. Venue view shows "Sign in as ... (demo)" and "Loading the schedule..." on first view.
- **The screenshots are good but dated.** The Activity, Plans and Map shots are clean and legible. They use "Alex" and Oct 30, whereas the live demo is now Priya and Oct 31. The Plans shot shows the Echo Karaoke booking in the no-friend-paid state, not the demo-panel flow. There is no shot of the drawer, the negotiation chart, the receipt, or any PayPal popup. The drawer is the feature a non-technical judge would most want to see.

## Scores

**Technological Implementation: 9/10**
- Strongest evidence: breadth and depth of PayPal use (authorize, partial final capture, void, refund, Payouts, Vault, Invoicing, Disputes evidence). JUDGING.md names the files. It also has idempotent PayPal request ids, 46 tests, MCP, REST and A2A with the same tools, mandate checks before a venue sees an offer, and signed receipts in a transparency log. The docs state honestly what has not run on the sandbox (webhooks, disputes, Pay Later).
- Weaknesses:
  - The scheduler crash above.
  - "Test card stand-in" means no judge sees a real PayPal approval screen.
  - Several claims (webhooks, disputes, the Claude examples) are "built against a stand-in," which a skeptic will discount.
  - Qwen 0.5B is a thin AI contribution, and the real AI is the user's own Claude, which Join does not ship.
  - Much of the stack (RFC 6962 log, C2SP witnesses, AP2, RFC 9421, WebMCP) reads as resume-padding to a non-engineer. Judges may not credit it.

**Design: 6/10**
- Strongest evidence: the dark UI is clean, the sidebar is clear, and Activity, Plans and the negotiation bar chart are legible. Code-written sentences are a distinctive trust choice. The drawer cards show reasons and counted review tags.
- Weaknesses:
  - The product has many surfaces and little guidance. Activity, Plans, Map, Limits, Connect, Venue view and a drawer are all competing. Nothing tells a new user which one to use first.
